Niagara Falls.wildlife_intro:
Niagara Falls keeps our crew busy with Norway rats and pigeons around the older downtown, raccoons along the gorge, and squirrels in the LaSalle canopy. Niagara River and the gorge  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Niagara Falls. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Niagara Falls jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Lockport is the Erie Canal's lock city — the famous Flight of Five climbs through its center — with a historic downtown of stone and brick, older neighborhoods on the escarpment, and subdivisions spreading east. Norway rats work the canal corridor, downtown cellars, and oldest housing; raccoons and squirrels fill the attics above them; and the escarpment's rocky, wooded face behind the city shelters everything else.

Lockport's two levels — canal level and escarpment level — run through its wildlife work as well: rats and foundation entries down low, attic tenants in the housing above, and skunks under porches in between. Our crew inspects Lockport homes at both levels, removes the animals, and seals accordingly, with canal-side properties getting the closest foundation attention our route offers anywhere.

faqs.q: What wildlife comes with living near the canal terminus?
faqs.a: Raccoons above all — the canal and river banks are their highway, and North Tonawanda's chimneys are a short walk from both. North Tonawanda.wildlife_intro:
North Tonawanda sits at the Erie Canal's western terminus, where Tonawanda Creek meets the Niagara River — a former lumber port of older neighborhoods, canal-side streets, and postwar subdivisions. Raccoons commute from the river and canal banks into its chimneys and attics, squirrels work the canopy of its older sections, and the creek corridor keeps skunks and opossums moving through the yards.

Water on two sides shapes North Tonawanda's inspections: river-edge and canal-edge homes see ground-level traffic that interior streets escape, so foundations, porches, and sheds join the roofline on the checklist. Our crew inspects North Tonawanda homes by their distance from the water, removes the animals, and seals or screens the levels the evidence supports — older lumber-era housing near the terminus gets the most complete version of the job.

Newfane.wildlife_intro:
Newfane is Niagara County's lake-plain farm town — orchards, vineyards, and field country running down to Lake Ontario at Olcott's little harbor. Its wildlife work is agricultural: groundhogs along the orchard rows and field edges, skunks and opossums around the farmsteads, and bats in the eaves of its older farmhouses. Olcott's cottages add a seasonal lake strip where closed houses collect winter tenants.

Fruit country feeds everything: dropped apples and grapes draw raccoons and skunks from midsummer to harvest, and the farm buildings give them daytime shelter a field away from the houses. Our crew treats Newfane properties whole — farmhouse proofing plus outbuilding screening — removes the animals, and checks the Olcott cottages at closing, because a lake cottage sealed in October is a service call avoided in May.
